rv.q: And I defy anyone not to shiver when this Cyrano, in the play’s penultimate scene, stands tall amid cannon and musket smoke, his arms raised to the heavens.

Not only is Jamie Lloyd's staging as noisy as a concert by a band of jackhammers, but the Roundabout's production makes use of a boisterous new rhyming translation by Ranjit Bolt that updates the play's language to inconsistent effect.
Clever as it seemed in the opening scenes, the concept soon overwhelms Rostand's high classical style and soaring poetry.
But while Hodge attacks the title role with formidable energy and inventiveness, his virtuosic display muffles the poetry of the play.
It looks like a blunt instrument, a quality shared with this new Roundabout revival as a whole.
As staged by Jamie Lloyd, this 'Cyrano' comes off as an irritating bore.
Alas, in most other ways, this is a busy, generic production.
These assets add up to the most exciting Broadway production of a pre-20th century classic since 2010's The Merchant of Venice — a winner by more than a nose.
I would urge everyone to check out Roundabout Theatre Company's thoughtful, committed production.
The tone is light, but not lightweight – you’ll laugh, but you’ll be moved too.
Hodge's participation is largely why this presentation is a pleasure to watch, especially in the quicker, better-paced second act, where his pre-death monologue becomes the show's defining moment.
If not great or memorable, it's good, and very solid.
But clarity would only have emphasized an adaptation peppered with anachronisms and banal rhymes.
For the rest of this eminently entertaining production, one is taken by Edmond Rostand‘s invigorating poetics, like verbal puzzles for which one waits for the punch line.

tn.cat: Best Costume Design of a Play

cn.t: Douglas Hodge's bracingly fresh, unconventional performance electrifies this production, though critics split on Jamie Lloyd's dark, rough-hewn staging—some find it thrillingly original, others miss the play's traditional elegance.

vs.sum: Completed a major renovation in early 2026 with all seats replaced and legroom expanded, making it one of Broadway's most comfortable and modern houses. New restrooms significantly reduce intermission wait times.

acc.note: Elevators to all levels. 53 assistive listening devices. 11 wheelchair seats across Orchestra and Balcony.
